blocks: Each subject completed two sessions of OVAR with either the active ITD (−7 cm H₂O inspiratory resistance) or SHAM (0 cm H₂O resistance).  A minimum of 7 days passed between sessions to minimize habituation to OVAR.

Subjects experienced the following protocol: 5 minutes to collect baseline data with no rotation, 15 minutes of OVAR (15 revolutions per minute at 15 degree tilt), followed by an additional 5 minutes of baseline with no rotation.  At 15 seconds before rotation, the subjects began breathing through either an active ITD or a control SHAM device.  A nose-clip was used to insure that subjects breathed through the device.  During rotation, subjects were asked to indicate their subjective symptoms according to the 5-level scale at minute intervals with their free hand.  The subjects were informed to terminate rotation once symptoms reached those of intense motion sickness (symptom level 5).  For subjects who had terminated rotation before the 15 minutes, a symptom level of 5 was recorded for the subsequent minute symptoms.  After each session, subjects completed a survey detailing their experienced symptoms.

Data was collected on the housed laptop using Windaq data acquisition software. A representative graph of mean CBFV is presented in Chart 1.  The diastolic and systolic points of the CBFV waveform and the minute symptoms were recorded and statistically analyzed using t-tests on Microsoft Excel.  For CBFV reductions, we used a one-tailed t-test to compare the significance of the difference between the mean baseline CBFV and the mean rotation CBFV with each device (i.e. how much lower is the mean CBFV for rotation than the mean CBFV for baseline on each device).  Since this change was defined to be directional—a reduction from baseline to rotation CBFV—we found the one-tailed t-test to be well-suited for statistical analysis of CBFV.³  For the analysis of non-directional subjective symptoms we used two-tailed t-tests comparing the means of the symptoms between the subjects using the ITD and SHAM.  A p-value of 0.05 was used to establish significance for statistical tests.
The ITD prevented a significant reduction in mean CBFV (Chart 2).

The results are displayed in Chart 2. The bars indicate the standard error.  Mean CBFV was calculated using the equation: CBFVmean = CBFVdias + 0.4(CBFVsys − CBFVdias).⁴  The subjects using the SHAM showed a significant decrease (p = 0.040) between baseline and rotation mean CBFV, while the subjects on the ITD did not have a significant decrease (p = 0.231).  We would expect the difference for the active ITD not to be significant as this shows that there was not a significant reduction in mean CBFV between baseline and rotation when on the ITD. The ITD does not appear to mitigate motion sickness symptoms (Charts 3, 4).

Mean minute symptoms are presented in Chart 3. The data shows there is no statistically significant difference (average p = 0.273) in the minute motion sickness symptoms for any minute between symptomatic subjects when on the ITD or SHAM.  Total mean motion sickness symptoms were calculated through the integration of the minute symptom curve and are presented in Chart 4.  Total symptoms also show no statistically significant difference between symptoms for the ITD and SHAM (p = 0.397). This indicates that though the ITD prevented a significant reduction in mean CBFV, motion sickness symptoms were not significantly alleviated.
